claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Response to In11 was observed in plant species within the broader monophyletic clade of the Phaseoloids.
claims.source: Response to In11 was observed in plant species within the broader monophyletic clade of the Phaseoloids.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ethylene accumulation data shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: Phylogenetic evidence suggests a single origin of In11 response at the base of the Phaseoloid legumes ~28 my ago.
claims.source: Hence, phylogenetic evidence suggests a single origin of In11 response at the base of the Phaseoloid legumes ~28 my ago (mya; Figure 1b, ★).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and phenotypic data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Several tested plant species/accessions within the Phaseoloid clade were unable to respond to In11, namely Hylodesmum podocarpum, winged bean (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus), soybean (Glycine max), yam bean (Pachyrhizus erosus), and calopo (Calopogonium mucunoides).
claims.source: Several of the tested plant species/accessions within this clade were unable to respond to In11, namely Hylodesmum podocarpum, winged bean (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus), soybean (Glycine max), yam bean (Pachyrhizus erosus), and calopo (Calopogonium mucunoides), although these species were able to respond to the unrelated bacterial PAMP flg22 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ethylene and ROS data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Species unable to respond to In11 were able to respond to the unrelated bacterial PAMP flg22.
claims.source: Several of the tested plant species/accessions within this clade were unable to respond to In11, namely Hylodesmum podocarpum, winged bean (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus), soybean (Glycine max), yam bean (Pachyrhizus erosus), and calopo (Calopogonium mucunoides), although these species were able to respond to the unrelated bacterial PAMP flg22 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ethylene and ROS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Multiple independent losses of In11 response occurred throughout Phaseoloid evolution after the initial emergence of this function.
claims.source: These observations suggest the occurrence of multiple independent losses of In11 response throughout Phaseoloid evolution after the initial emergence of this function.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that several Phaseoloid species cannot respond to In11.

claims.claim: The organization of the INR locus is highly diverse among legumes, with zero to seven LRR-RLP encoding-genes per species in addition to extensive repetitive sequence and transposable element content.
claims.source: The organization of the INR locus is highly diverse among legumes, with zero to seven LRR-RLP encoding-genes per species in addition to extensive repetitive sequence and transposable element content (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 6c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: BLASTN search did not identify any regions with higher score than sequences at the contiguous INR locus of the respective species, strongly suggesting that all potential INR homologs are encoded at this syntenic locus.
claims.source: For all species, BLASTN search did not identify any regions with higher score than sequences at the contiguous INR locus of the respective species, strongly suggesting that all potential INR homologs are encoded at this syntenic locus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by BLASTN analysis of genome sequences.

claims.claim: Legume species within the Hologalegina, namely Lotus angustifolius, chickpea (Cicer arietinum), Medicago truncatula, and clover (Trifolium pratense) do not contain an LRR-RLP encoding gene at the locus.
claims.source: Legume species within the Hologalegina, namely Lotus angustifolius, chickpea (Cicer arietinum), Medicago truncatula, and clover (Trifolium pratense) do not contain an LRR-RLP encoding gene at the locus, whereas all species within the Millettioids except for P. erosus contained at least one LRR-RLP, consistent with a gene insertion event of an LRR-RLP at the INR locus in the ancestor of extant Millettioids (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: All species within the Millettioids except for P. erosus contained at least one LRR-RLP at the INR locus.
claims.source: Legume species within the Hologalegina, namely Lotus angustifolius, chickpea (Cicer arietinum), Medicago truncatula, and clover (Trifolium pratense) do not contain an LRR-RLP encoding gene at the locus, whereas all species within the Millettioids except for P. erosus contained at least one LRR-RLP, consistent with a gene insertion event of an LRR-RLP at the INR locus in the ancestor of extant Millettioids (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: A gene insertion event of an LRR-RLP at the INR locus occurred in the ancestor of extant Millettioids.
claims.source: Legume species within the Hologalegina, namely Lotus angustifolius, chickpea (Cicer arietinum), Medicago truncatula, and clover (Trifolium pratense) do not contain an LRR-RLP encoding gene at the locus, whereas all species within the Millettioids except for P. erosus contained at least one LRR-RLP, consistent with a gene insertion event of an LRR-RLP at the INR locus in the ancestor of extant Millettioids (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of LRR-RLPs in Millettioids but not in Hologalegina.

claims.claim: C. tetragonoloba is a close outgroup of Millettioid legumes.
claims.source: To investigate this emergence, we analyzed the de novo assembly of C. tetragonoloba, a close outgroup of Millettioid legumes (Figure 1b; Cardoso et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cardoso et al., 2015 and Zhao et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Neither LRR-RLP was present between the anchor genes in C. tetragonoloba nor was an LRR-RLP with greater than 68% similarity found in the whole genome.
claims.source: As with all species in the outgroup Hologalegina, neither LRR-RLP was present between the anchor genes in C. tetragonoloba nor did we find an LRR-RLP with greater than 68% similarity in the whole genome, strengthening support for a single ancestral LRR-RLP gene insertion event ~32 mya (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. tetragonoloba genome assembly.

claims.claim: The absence of LRR-RLP in C. tetragonoloba strengthens support for a single ancestral LRR-RLP gene insertion event ~32 mya.
claims.source: As with all species in the outgroup Hologalegina, neither LRR-RLP was present between the anchor genes in C. tetragonoloba nor did we find an LRR-RLP with greater than 68% similarity in the whole genome, strengthening support for a single ancestral LRR-RLP gene insertion event ~32 mya (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of LRR-RLP in outgroup species.

claims.claim: BLASTN analysis of the contiguous INR locus of P. erosus revealed only partial coding sequence fragments with homology to LRR-RLPs, and consequently the absence of an INR homolog.
claims.source: In contrast to other closely related legume species, BLASTN analysis of the contiguous INR locus of P. erosus revealed only partial coding sequence fragments with homology to LRR-RLPs, and consequently the absence of an INR homolog (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BLASTN analysis and shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: The de novo assembly of the P. erosus INR locus was validated by performing PCR spanning the complete disruption and Sanger sequencing of the resulting amplicon.
claims.source: The de novo assembly of the locus was validated by performing PCR spanning the complete disruption and Sanger sequencing of the resulting amplicon.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PCR and Sanger sequencing data.

claims.claim: A Mariner-like transposase element exists between the LRR-RLP gene fragments in P. erosus.
claims.source: A Mariner-like transposase element exists between the LRR-RLP gene fragments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1,Supplementary file 6c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transposable element analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The absence of an INR homolog in P. erosus corresponds with species phenotype, namely the lack of induced ethylene response after In11 treatment.
claims.source: The absence of an INR homolog in P. erosus corresponds with species phenotype, namely the lack of induced ethylene response after In11 treatment (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 1a and genomic data shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: A single well-supported clade which includes the previously characterized functional INR from V. unguiculata (Vigun07g219600) also contained orthologs from plant species able to respond to In11.
claims.source: A single well-supported clade which includes the previously characterized functional INR from V. unguiculata (Vigun07g219600) also contained orthologs from plant species able to respond to In11 (Figure 3a; Steinbrenner et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3a and citation to Steinbrenner et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The INR clade contains functional INR homologs which can confer In11-induced functions.
claims.source: Hence, we hypothesized that this clade contains functional INR homologs which can confer In11-induced functions.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Five genes (Vigun07g219600, Phvul.007G077500, Mlathy INR, C.cajan_07316, and Mprur INR) within the INR clade were cloned and transiently expressed in N. benthamiana.
claims.source: To validate the putative INR clade, five genes (Vigun07g219600, Phvul.007G077500, Mlathy INR, C.cajan_07316, and Mprur INR) within this clade were cloned and transiently expressed in the non-legume model species N. benthamiana.
claims.evidence: This is a description of experimental methods.

claims.claim: In11-induced ethylene and ROS production were able to be conferred by each of the five tested INR clade genes.
claims.source: In11-induced ethylene and ROS production were able to be conferred by each gene (Figure 3b–c), consistent with novel In11 recognition enabled by the INR clade (Figure 3a, blue labels).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ethylene and ROS data shown in Figure 3b-c.

claims.claim: Cyclic ROS responses were observed for three out of five In11 responding receptors (Vigun07g219600, Phvul.007G077500, and Mlathy INR).
claims.source: Intriguingly, cyclic ROS responses were observed for three out of five In11 responding receptors (Vigun07g219600, Phvul.007G077500, and Mlathy INR).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ROS data shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Constructs without a C-terminal GFP tag reduced cyclic characteristics of the ROS response but resulted in equivalent ethylene bursts.
claims.source: Corresponding constructs without a C-terminal GFP tag reduced cyclic characteristics of the ROS response but resulted in equivalent ethylene bursts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: No In11-induced responses could be observed upon heterologous expression of Vigun07g219700, Glyma.10G228000, Vigun07g039700, and Phvul.007g246600.
claims.source: No In11-induced responses could be observed upon heterologous expression of Vigun07g219700, Glyma.10G228000, Vigun07g039700, and Phvul.007g246600 (Figure 3b–c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ethylene and ROS data shown in Figure 3b-c.

claims.claim: Proteins of non-responsive LRR-RLPs were similarly or more strongly expressed in N. benthamiana relative to the lowest expressed responsive LRR-RLP (C.cajan_07316 INR), except for the marginally lower expressed Vigun07g039700.
claims.source: Proteins of these non-responsive LRR-RLPs were similarly or more strongly expressed in N. benthamiana relative to the lowest expressed responsive LRR-RLP (C.cajan_07316 INR; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), except for the marginally lower expressed Vigun07g039700, which contrasts with its closest related gene in P. vulgaris (Phvul.007g246600, 87% AA similarity).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The ability to confer In11-induced ROS and ethylene production is strictly limited to members of the INR clade.
claims.source: Thus, the ability to confer In11-induced ROS and ethylene production is strictly limited to members of the INR clade.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only INR clade members confer In11 response.

claims.claim: Reconciliation analysis between gene and species trees revealed a complex evolutionary history comprising 19 gene duplications and 20 gene losses in total.
claims.source: Reconciliation analysis between gene and species trees revealed a complex evolutionary history comprising 19 gene duplications and 20 gene losses in total.
claims.evidence: This is supported by NOTUNG analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Within the Millettioids, a single duplication event gave rise to the INR clade containing all INR homologs and its sister clade which contains the closest related INR-like homologs.
claims.source: Within the Millettioids, a single duplication event gave rise to the INR clade containing all INR homologs and its sister clade which contains the closest related INR-like homologs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by NOTUNG analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: P. vulgaris and Mucuna pruriens contain an INR clade homolog but not members of the sister INR-like 1 clade, consistent with two independent gene losses.
claims.source: P. vulgaris and Mucuna pruriens contain an INR clade homolog but not members of the sister INR-like 1 clade, consistent with two independent gene losses.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic and genomic analysis.

claims.claim: The analysis predicts the ancestral loss of an INR homolog within the INR clade for G. soja, G. max, and H. podocarpum and clade specific duplication events resulting in LRR-RLP expansions of 4–7 tandem duplicates.
claims.source: In contrast, the analysis predicts the ancestral loss of an INR homolog within the INR clade for G. soja, G. max, and H. podocarpum and clade specific duplication events resulting in LRR-RLP expansions of 4–7 tandem duplicates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by NOTUNG analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: No BLASTP hits to Vu07g219600 for any of the 26 de novo assemblies of G. soja and G. max were identified that had an AA similarity higher than 76%, suggesting that INR was lost before the speciation of G. max and G. soja.
claims.source: To confirm that INR was lost in Glycine and not just in reference assemblies, we performed BLASTP searches using Vigun07g219700 AA sequence against 26 G. soja and G. max de novo assemblies from a recent pangenome analysis (Liu et al., 2020). Like the Glycine reference genomes, no BLASTP hits to Vu07g219600 for any of the 26 de novo assemblies were identified that had an AA similarity higher than 76%, suggesting that INR was lost before the speciation of G. max and G. soja, i.e., prior to soybean domestication.
claims.evidence: This is supported by BLASTP analysis of 26 Glycine genomes.

claims.claim: INR was lost prior to soybean domestication.
claims.source: To confirm that INR was lost in Glycine and not just in reference assemblies, we performed BLASTP searches using Vigun07g219700 AA sequence against 26 G. soja and G. max de novo assemblies from a recent pangenome analysis (Liu et al., 2020). Like the Glycine reference genomes, no BLASTP hits to Vu07g219600 for any of the 26 de novo assemblies were identified that had an AA similarity higher than 76%, suggesting that INR was lost before the speciation of G. max and G. soja, i.e., prior to soybean domestication.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of INR in both G. soja and G. max.

claims.claim: All identified INR homologs encode a cytoplasmic tail of only 10 AA, shorter relative to all identified INR-like homologs.
claims.source: Strikingly, all identified INR homologs encode a cytoplasmic tail of only 10 AA, shorter relative to all identified INR-like homologs here.
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis of INR and INR-like homologs.

claims.claim: Swapping the VuINR (Vigun07g219600) cytoplasmic tail to the extended version of VuINR-like 1 (Vigun07g219700), 219600 F, did not affect In11-response.
claims.source: Nevertheless, swapping the VuINR (Vigun07g219600) cytoplasmic tail to the extended version of VuINR-like 1 (Vigun07g219700), 219600 F, did not affect In11-response (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Chimeric receptors with the VuINR-like C1 domain were not responsive to In11.
claims.source: Chimeric receptors with the VuINR-like C1 domain were not responsive to In11.
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: All chimeric receptors containing the C1-C2 of VuINR responded to In11 treatment with both an ethylene and ROS burst (219600 F, 219600-C3, 219600-C2, and C1-219600).
claims.source: In contrast, all chimeric receptors containing the C1-C2 of VuINR responded to In11 treatment with both an ethylene and ROS burst (219600 F, 219600-C3, 219600-C2, and C1-219600; Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The chimeric receptor 219600−C1, containing C1 of VuINR and C2 of VuINR-like, responded to the control treatment.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the chimeric receptor 219600−C1, containing C1 of VuINR and C2 of VuINR-like, responded to the control treatment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: No visible phenotype was observed 7 days post-infiltration of 219600-C1 in N. benthamiana with or without subsequent infiltration of flg22, In11, or H2O 1 day post the construct infiltration.
claims.source: Nonetheless, no visible phenotype was observed 7 days post-infiltration of 219600-C1 in N. benthamiana with or without subsequent infiltration of flg22, In11, or H2O 1 day post the construct infiltration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–2b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by visual observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The chimeric receptor, 219600−C2, responds to In11 but has a delayed ROS burst relative to all other In11-responsive constructs tested.
claims.source: Additionally, the chimeric receptor, 219600−C2, responds to In11 but has a delayed ROS burst relative to all other In11-responsive constructs tested.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ROS data shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: The VuINR LRR subdomains C1 and C2 are both required for In11 response in chimeric receptors.
claims.source: In summary, the VuINR LRR subdomains C1 and C2 are both required for In11 response in chimeric receptors.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chimeric receptors with both C1 and C2 from VuINR respond to In11.

claims.claim: Ancestral receptors to the INR clade of the Vigna, Phaseolus, and Macroptylium (N7), the Phaseolinae (N6) and the Phaseoloids (N4) conferred In11-induced ethylene and ROS response.
claims.source: Ancestral receptors to the INR clade of the Vigna, Phaseolus, and Macroptylium (N7), the Phaseolinae (N6) and the Phaseoloids (N4) conferred In11-induced ethylene and ROS response.
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 5c-d.

claims.claim: Ancestral receptors of the INR-like 1 clade of the Phaseolinae (N16) and the Phaseoloids (N14) were not responsive to In11.
claims.source: In contrast, ancestral receptors of the INR-like 1 clade of the Phaseolinae (N16) and the Phaseoloids (N14) were not responsive to In11 (Figure 5d, Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 5c-d.

claims.claim: The common ancestral receptor of the INR and its INR-like 1 sister clade (N3) is not responsive to In11.
claims.source: Moreover, the common ancestral receptor of the INR and its INR-like 1 sister clade (N3) is not responsive to In11 (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 5c-d.

claims.claim: 16 of 720 AA differences between the LRR domain of N3 and N4 mediate differential In11 response.
claims.source: Hence, a small number of differences, 16 of 720 AA, between the LRR domain of N3 and N4, mediate differential In11 response.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that N3 and N4 differ in In11 response and have 16 AA differences.

claims.claim: Only a subset of the 16 AA differences is similar within all LRR-RLPs of the INR clade and different in LRR-RLPs of the INR-like 1 sister clade: Y91, H239, A359, H404, and R406.
claims.source: Moreover, only a subset of those AAs is similar within all LRR-RLPs of the INR clade and different in LRR-RLPs of the INR-like 1 sister clade: Y91, H239, A359, H404, and R406 (Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claims.claim: Reconstruction of ancestral INR homologs pinpoints a limited number of SNPs which mediate In11 recognition.
claims.source: Thus, reconstruction of ancestral INR homologs pinpoints a limited number of SNPs which mediate In11 recognition.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ASR analysis and identification of key amino acids.

claims.claim: N4 H239D and N4 A359S responded to In11 treatment with both an ethylene and ROS burst.
claims.source: N4 H239D and N4 A359S responded to In11 treatment with both an ethylene and ROS burst (Figure 6c–d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 6c-d.

claims.claim: N4 Y91F responded to In11 treatment although with a relatively lower ROS burst.
claims.source: Similarly, N4 Y91F responded to In11 treatment although with a relatively lower ROS burst.
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 6c-d.

claims.claim: N4 H404N and N4 R406K did not respond to In11.
claims.source: Finally, N4 H404N and N4 R406K did not respond to In11, allowing us to pinpoint to two AA substitutions which appeared to be crucial in the evolution of INR function.
claims.evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 6c-d.

claims.claim: Two AA substitutions, H404N and R406K, appeared to be crucial in the evolution of INR function.
claims.source: Finally, N4 H404N and N4 R406K did not respond to In11, allowing us to pinpoint to two AA substitutions which appeared to be crucial in the evolution of INR function.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these substitutions abolish In11 response.

claims.claim: The In11 peptide (sequence ICDINGVCVDA) is a host derived proteolytic fragment of the ATP synthase γ-subunit (cATPC), based on the V. unguiculata cATPC sequence.
claims.source: The In11 peptide (sequence ICDINGVCVDA) is a host derived proteolytic fragment of the ATP synthase γ-subunit (cATPC), based on the V. unguiculata cATPC sequence (Schmelz et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmelz et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The flg22 peptide (sequence QRLSTGSRINSAKDDAAGLQIA) originates from bacterial flagellin.
claims.source: The flg22 peptide (sequence QRLSTGSRINSAKDDAAGLQIA) originates from bacterial flagellin (Felix et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Felix et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Response to In11 was previously thought to be highly restricted since only species in a subtribe of legumes, the Phaseolinae, which includes the species cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) and common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris), encode the corresponding INR receptor.
claims.source: Response to the peptide HAMP In11 was previously thought to be highly restricted since only species in a subtribe of legumes, the Phaseolinae, which includes the species cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) and common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris), encode the corresponding INR receptor (Steinbrenner et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinbrenner et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Each of 364 tested varieties of V. unguiculata are able to respond to In11.
claims.source: Each of 364 tested varieties of V. unguiculata are able to respond to In11 and our analysis now extends this conservation across legume species (Steinbrenner et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinbrenner et al., 2020.

claims.claim: INR most likely arose from an existing LRR-RLP, ~28 mya.
claims.source: Certain Phaseoloids and earlier diverged non-Phaseoloids also contain INR-like homologs at the contiguous INR locus; thus, INR most likely arose from an existing LRR-RLP, ~28 mya.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of INR-like homologs in non-Phaseoloids.

claims.claim: The role of INR-like homologs is not clear, but they may detect a related, In11-like ligand.
claims.source: The role of INR-like homologs is not clear, but they may detect a related, In11-like ligand.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the potential function of INR-like homologs.

claims.claim: The evolutionary pattern of INR is reminiscent of the evolution of LRR-RLP Cf-2 which evolved <6 mya within the genus Solanum, potentially by intergenic recombination.
claims.source: This evolutionary pattern is reminiscent of the evolution of LRR-RLP Cf-2 which evolved <6 mya within the genus Solanum, potentially by intergenic recombination (Kourelis et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kourelis et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The high level of AA conservation of the recognized ligand In11 may drive overall stability of the INR locus since the divergence of the Phaseoloids ~28 mya.
claims.source: The high level of AA conservation of the recognized ligand In11 (Schmelz et al., 2006) may drive overall stability of the INR locus since the divergence of the Phaseoloids ~28 mya.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between ligand conservation and locus stability, supported by citation to Schmelz et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Two reference genomes as well as 26 de novo assemblies of the closely related Glycininae, G. soja and G. max, do not encode INR.
claims.source: Two reference genomes as well as 26 de novo assemblies of the closely related Glycininae, G. soja and G. max, do not encode INR (Liu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claims.claim: INR loss does not seem to predate the divergence of the Glycininae as Teramnus labialis is able to respond to In11.
claims.source: Nevertheless, INR loss does not seem to predate the divergence of the Glycininae as Teramnus labialis is able to respond to In11 (Figure 1), although genome data are lacking for this species.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that T. labialis responds to In11.

claims.claim: Gene tree-species tree reconciliation suggests the involvement of five tandem duplications of an INR-like gene predating radiation of the genus Glycine.
claims.source: Besides reciprocal gene loss of INR, gene tree-species tree reconciliation also suggests the involvement of five tandem duplications of an INR-like gene predating radiation of the genus Glycine (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by NOTUNG analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Whole-genome observations show preferential gene loss in tandem clusters.
claims.source: This is consistent with whole-genome observations of preferential gene loss in tandem clusters (Shi et al., 2014).

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background knowledge about PRRs, their structure, function, and lineage-specific evolution in plants. PRRs, particularly LRR-RLPs, are germline-encoded receptors that recognize PAMPs, HAMPs, and DAMPs. These receptors show lineage-specific functions across plant families, but the specific evolutionary steps leading to novel LRR-RLP functions have not been well described.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C33 collectively establish well-supported background knowledge about PRR structure, function, and evolution, primarily through citations to prior literature. These claims appropriately frame the knowledge gap (C2, C30) that motivates the current study. The claims are consistent with established understanding in the field.

results.result: In11 recognition is restricted to the Phaseoloid legume clade, with a single origin approximately 28 million years ago. The authors tested 22 legume species and found that In11 response was observed only in Phaseoloid species, though several Phaseoloid species showed loss of In11 response, suggesting multiple independent losses after the initial emergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C38-C42 are well-supported by ethylene accumulation data across 22 legume species (Figure 1) and phylogenetic analysis. The data clearly show In11 response restricted to Phaseoloids with appropriate controls (flg22 response in C41). The inference of single origin and multiple losses (C39, C42) is reasonable given the phylogenetic distribution.

results.result: The INR locus shows high diversity among legumes with 0-7 LRR-RLP genes per species. Hologalegina species lack LRR-RLPs at this locus, while Millettioids (except P. erosus) contain at least one LRR-RLP, consistent with a gene insertion event ~32 million years ago. P. erosus shows a disrupted INR locus with only partial gene fragments and a transposable element insertion.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C54 are strongly supported by comparative genomic analysis across 20 legume species (Figure 2). The P. erosus disruption is validated by multiple methods including PCR and Sanger sequencing (C52). The correlation between INR absence and lack of In11 response in P. erosus (C54) provides functional validation of the genomic findings.

results.result: A single phylogenetic clade of INR homologs from Phaseoloid species is functional for In11 recognition. Five genes from this clade conferred In11-induced ethylene and ROS production when heterologously expressed in N. benthamiana, while four genes outside this clade did not confer In11 response despite similar or higher expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C63 are well-supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3a) and functional validation in N. benthamiana (Figure 3b-c). The inclusion of expression controls (C62, western blot data) strengthens the conclusion that lack of response is not due to poor expression. The observation of cyclic ROS responses (C59-C60) is interesting but does not affect the main conclusion about functional specificity.

results.result: Gene tree-species tree reconciliation revealed complex evolutionary history with 19 duplications and 20 losses. A single duplication event gave rise to the INR clade and its sister clade. Multiple independent losses occurred, including loss of INR in Glycine (G. max and G. soja) prior to domestication, confirmed across 26 de novo genome assemblies.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 are supported by NOTUNG analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and extensive BLASTP searches across 26 Glycine genomes. The inference that INR loss preceded domestication (C69) is well-supported by the absence of INR in both wild (G. soja) and domesticated (G. max) species. The reconciliation analysis appropriately accounts for the complex evolutionary dynamics at this locus.

results.result: Chimeric receptor analysis revealed that the C1 and C2 LRR subdomains of VuINR are both required for In11 response. All chimeric receptors containing both C1-C2 from VuINR responded to In11, while those with VuINR-like C1 did not respond. The short cytoplasmic tail of INR is not essential for function.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C77 are well-supported by systematic chimeric receptor analysis (Figure 4) with appropriate functional assays (ROS and ethylene). The observation that the cytoplasmic tail swap does not affect function (C71) is clearly demonstrated. The unusual response of 219600-C1 to control treatment (C74) is noted but does not produce visible phenotype (C75), suggesting it may be an artifact. Overall, the domain mapping is convincing.

results.result: Ancestral sequence reconstruction showed that the ancestral receptor N4 (common ancestor of INR clade) conferred In11 response, while N3 (common ancestor of INR and INR-like clades) did not. Only 16 amino acid differences between N3 and N4 mediate differential In11 response, with 5 amino acids showing 100% conservation across all INR clade members.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 are strongly supported by ASR analysis and functional testing of reconstructed receptors (Figure 5). The phylogenetic trees show good bootstrap support for the reconstructed nodes. The functional data clearly demonstrate that N4 responds to In11 while N3 does not, and the identification of 16 key amino acids (C81-C82) is based on sequence alignment. This represents a powerful application of ASR to identify functional determinants.

results.result: Site-directed mutagenesis of N4 identified two critical amino acid substitutions (H404N and R406K) that abolish In11 response. Three other substitutions (Y91F, H239D, A359S) maintained In11 response, though Y91F showed reduced ROS burst.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are well-supported by functional testing of N4 variants (Figure 6). The identification of H404 and R406 as critical residues is clear from the loss-of-function phenotype. The observation that Y91F shows reduced but not abolished response (C85) suggests this residue may modulate but not determine specificity. The conclusion that these substitutions were crucial for INR evolution (C87) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: The manuscript contextualizes the INR system within broader evolutionary and methodological frameworks. ASR is a powerful but underutilized approach for studying PRR evolution. INR likely arose from an existing LRR-RLP ~28 mya, and its evolution may be driven by ligand conservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 and C90-C95 provide appropriate context and interpretation. The statements about ASR (C34-C36) are supported by citations. The speculation about INR origin (C92-C93) and ligand-driven stability (C95) are reasonable interpretations marked as inference or speculation. These contextual claims appropriately frame the significance of the findings.

results.result: Multiple independent losses of INR occurred in different lineages through various mechanisms. Glycine lost INR before speciation, H. podocarpum underwent tandem duplications after INR loss, and P. erosus lost both INR and INR-like genes. Transposable elements may have contributed to gene disruption.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C104 are supported by genomic analysis across multiple species and pangenome data. The inference of different evolutionary trajectories in different lineages (C98, C100) is well-supported by phylogenetic and genomic evidence. The speculation about transposable element involvement (C103) is appropriately marked and supported by the presence of TEs at disrupted loci. The citation to support preferential loss in tandem clusters (C99, C104) provides appropriate context.

results.result: The authors discuss the need for similar evolutionary analyses in other plant families, particularly Brassicaceae, where extensive phenotyping exists but locus-level analysis has not been conducted. Additional case studies are needed to reveal broader patterns in PRR evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 appropriately discuss future directions and the broader implications of the work. The statements about Brassicaceae (C105-C108) are supported by citations and represent reasonable suggestions for future research. The call for additional case studies (C109) is appropriate given the novelty of the approach.

results.result: The importance of C1 and C2 domains for LRR-RLP function is consistent across multiple plant families and receptors (RLP23, RLP42, RXEG1, INR). However, the specific molecular mechanisms of PAMP/HAMP recognition by these domains require further investigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 synthesize findings from multiple studies (supported by citations) with the current work to identify common patterns. The inference that C1 and C2 are generally critical (C113) is well-supported by convergent evidence from multiple systems. The acknowledgment that mechanistic details remain unclear (C114) is appropriate.

results.result: The cytoplasmic tail of LRR-RLPs appears to have auxiliary rather than essential function, based on studies of RLP23 and RLP42 showing that tail deletion or replacement reduces but does not abolish receptor function.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by citations to prior work and are consistent with the current findings on INR (C71). The interpretation of auxiliary function is reasonable given the quantitative rather than qualitative effects of tail modifications.

results.result: The ancestral receptors N3 and N4 differ by only 16 amino acids, with 5 showing 100% conservation in the INR clade. Two substitutions (H404N and R406K) are critical for INR function, representing key evolutionary changes that enabled In11 recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 integrate ASR and mutagenesis data to identify the minimal genetic changes underlying functional evolution. The data clearly support that these specific substitutions are critical (C121-C122). This represents a major finding about the molecular basis of evolutionary innovation in PRRs.

results.result: Evidence is accumulating across multiple LRR-RLPs (INR, RLP42) that specific residues in C1 and C2 domains play critical roles in ligand-specific responses, with single amino acid changes sufficient to abolish function.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 synthesize findings from the current work with prior studies (supported by citation) to identify general principles. The inference is well-supported by convergent evidence from multiple receptor systems.

results.result: The successful application of ASR to the relatively long INR LRR domain (720 AA) demonstrates the power of this approach for identifying key residues in PRRs without structural data. This approach may be broadly useful for studying PRR evolution and function.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C129 appropriately contextualize the methodological contribution of the work. The comparison to Pik-1 HMA (C125-C127, supported by citation) provides validation for the approach. The inference that ASR is powerful for long domains (C128) is supported by the successful identification of functional residues. The speculation about broader utility (C129) is appropriately marked and reasonable.

results.result: The In11 peptide is a host-derived proteolytic fragment of ATP synthase γ-subunit, while flg22 originates from bacterial flagellin. These represent the HAMP and PAMP used in the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 provide essential methodological context supported by appropriate citations. These are well-established facts about the peptides used in the study.
